Performance measures were the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the average precision score (APS). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) described model contributions, including paired vaccination-input changes in 2024. Findings: Annual national hospitalisation prevalence ranged from 1.01% to 1.60%. With all variables, mean cross-validation AUROC and APS were 0.8430 and 0.1283 for LightGBM (LGB), and 0.8415 and 0.1285 for XGBoost (XGB). Adding both morbidity indices to the demographics increased LGB APS from 0.0720 to 0.1158; adding vaccination further increased it to 0.1283. Next-year AUROC and APS averaged 0.8429 and 0.1267 for LGB and 0.8423 and 0.1277 for XGB. Age and morbidity were the most influential variables. Among vaccinated individuals, SHAP analysis indicated that vaccination contributed most strongly towards lower model-estimated hospitalisation risk in the oldest age group. Interpretation: Combining historical morbidity and vaccination information in gradient boosting models improved the ability to distinguish between people who experienced respiratory hospitalisation and those who did not in annual New Zealand population data. Similar next-year performance and interpretable variation across age and morbidity profiles support further development toward practical risk assessment, including calibration and evaluation across population groups.

items.title: Androgen Receptor SUMO site mutations ameliorate toxicity in Drosophila models of SBMA
items.abstract_or_text: Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA) is an X-linked neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the androgen receptor (AR) gene that produces a toxic, polyglutamine-expanded protein. SBMA is part of a broader class of polyglutamine (polyQ) diseases characterized by protein misfolding, aggregation, and progressive neuronal dysfunction, for which no disease-modifying therapies exist. Post-translational modification of AR, including SUMOylation, is an important regulator of its transcriptional activity, stability, and cellular localization. Disease protein modification by SUMO is implicated in various neurodegenerative diseases and can influence protein aggregation and toxicity in polyQ disorders. Prior studies suggest that preventing AR SUMOylation positively modifies disease phenotypes. Here, we generated Drosophila models expressing polyQ-expanded human AR in which the canonical SUMO acceptor lysine sites were mutated into arginines to prevent SUMOylation of AR. Using tissue-specific expression in neurons and muscle, we assessed effects on lifespan, motor behavior, AR localization, and gene expression. Mutation of AR SUMOylation sites leads to improvements in longevity when expressed in muscle. Effects on motor performance were more limited. Transcriptomic analysis revealed tissue-specific effects of AR SUMO-site mutation, with enrichment of immune, metabolic, and defense-related processes in heads, but limited enrichment in thoraces. In both tissues, a subset of genes altered by AR SUMO-site mutation showed expression changes opposing those associated with polyQ expansion. These findings support a modulatory role for SUMOylation in SBMA pathogenesis and highlight post-translational regulation of AR as a potential therapeutic avenue requiring further investigation.

items.title: Pruning the Search, Not the Signal: Adaptive-Banding Needleman-Wunsch Sequence Alignment via Protein Language Model Confidence
items.abstract_or_text: Dynamic programming (DP) yields exact quadratic-time (O(NM)) pairwise sequence alignments. Static banding heuristics (O(NW)) fail catastrophically on low-identity ( 98.9% of exact unconstrained alignment scores and core-block SP accuracy across static banding failure modes (Twilight Zone, Asymmetric Indels, Extreme Aspect Ratios) while eliminating 55.3%-78.8% of active DP cells. On large protein sequence matrices (N, M >= 3,700), AB-NW eliminates 87.6%-91.7% of cells, achieving speedups of 9.79x-13.30x (pure DP) and 1.73x-2.94x (end-to-end), reaching up to 18.12x on unbiased controls (p < 0.05 to p < 10^-15), making AB-NW practical for large-scale, high-throughput sequence alignment pipelines.

items.title: Predicting the impact of primaquine on Plasmodium falciparum transmission using multiscale modelling
items.abstract_or_text: Primaquine is currently the only widely available antimalarial drug that targets mature Plasmodium falciparum gametocytes, the life stage in the human bloodstream that mediates transmission from humans to mosquitoes. The only study that provided large-scale field data suitable for examining the additional impact of the WHO-recommended dose of 0.25 mg/kg primaquine in an artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT)-based mass drug administration (MDA) campaign was reported by Deng et al. (2018, Clinical Infectious Diseases). The study showed that both ACT alone and ACT plus primaquine substantially reduced average monthly malaria hospital rates and the prevalence of infection after the MDA campaign but no additional benefit was observed with primaquine. These findings challenge our expectations for the population-level impacts of primaquine and are in stark contrast to the predictions (of substantial population-level impacts) made by existing epidemiological-scale modelling studies. To address these knowledge gaps, we hypothesised that individuals' adherence patterns to multi-round MDA campaigns could be a factor that explains these conflicting empirical observations. To examine this hypothesis, we developed a data-driven multiscale agent-based model of malaria infection and transmission, which quantitatively captures both the detailed biology of human infection kinetics and the pharmacodynamic actions of antimalarial drugs. Our model provides a coherent explanation for these apparently disparate observations, including the individual-level gametocytocidal effect of primaquine, the population-level impacts of primaquine in MDA campaigns, and the population-level impacts predicted by previous modelling studies. All three observations can be explained by underlying adherence patterns within a single modelling framework. We used our model to predict the effect of primaquine in routine case management outside MDA, finding that administration could significantly reduce the prevalence of infection, supporting its use as a transmission-blocking intervention against malaria.

items.title: Predicting HPV/p16 Status and Molecular Subtypes from Histopathology Slides using Deep Learning in Vulvar Squamous Cell Carcinoma
items.abstract_or_text: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (VSCC) comprises three prognostically distinct molecular subtypes: human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated, HPV-independent/p53-wildtype, and HPV-independent/p53-abnormal. Classification requires p16/p53 immunohistochemistry, which consumes tissue and is often incomplete in retrospective cohorts. We investigated whether deep learning could predict HPV/p16 status and molecular subtypes directly from routine hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images. Using features extracted with H-optimus-1, we developed two attention-based multiple-instance learning models: HERA, predicting HPV/p16 status, and HERMES, predicting the three molecular subtypes. Models were developed on 644 patients from three Dutch VSCC cohorts and tested on 286 patients from two independent cohorts. In independent testing, HERA achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.84 (95% CI 0.75-0.91), with specificity 0.93, negative predictive value 0.94, and sensitivity 0.68. HERA-predicted groups reproduced the prognostic separation of HPV testing (log-rank p<0.001). HERMES achieved a macro-average AUC of 0.70 (0.66-0.75), with good discrimination for HPV-associated (0.80) but limited separation of HPV-independent/p53-abnormal (AUC 0.68) and HPV-independent/p53-wildtype (AUC 0.63). HERMES-predicted classes reproduced the prognostic hierarchy, with 5-year recurrence rates of 14.0% (HPV-associated), 31.1% (HPV-independent/p53-wildtype) and 43.3% (HPV-independent/p53-abnormal) (p=0.0051). Highly attended tiles showed basaloid cells and koilocytotic-like atypia in HPV-associated tumors, keratinizing nests with desmoplastic stroma in HPV-independent/p53-abnormal tumors, and well-differentiated keratinocytes with spongiosis in HPV-independent/p53-wildtype tumors. HERA could assign HPV/p16 status to large retrospective VSCC cohorts lacking ancillary testing, without consuming tissue, enabling HPV-stratified outcome analyses. Before such use, external validation of its discrimination and calibration across scanners and populations is required. HERMES suggests that molecular subtype information is encoded in hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides, but requires improved distinction between the HPV-independent subtypes.

items.title: Editorial: Imaging biomarkers in neurodegenerative diseases: advances and challenges
AI-Assisted Writing Across Medical Journals: Heterogeneity in Prevalence and Trends
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Estimates of generative artificial intelligence (AI) use in the medical literature vary widely, potentially reflecting differences across journals. We estimated changes in the prevalence of AI-generated writing over time using abstracts from 12 general medical journals. Methods: We randomly sampled up to 200 abstracts per journal-year from publications dated January 1, 2020, through August 8, 2026. Abstracts were scored using GPTZero, with journal-specific thresholds calibrated to fix a 1% false-positive rate (FPR) in the pre-AI baseline period (2020-2021). We estimated annual detector-positive proportions and calculated a publication-volume-weighted estimate across sampled journals. Associations with journal impact factor, publication model, and publication volume were examined descriptively. Results: Among 15,268 abstracts, estimated prevalence of AI-generated text increased after 2022, with substantial variation in timing and magnitude across journals. In 2026 through August 8, prevalence estimates ranged from 5.7% (95% CI, 2.1%-10.0%) in the New England Journal of Medicine to 83.5% (95% CI, 77.1%-87.5%) in Frontiers in Medicine. The publication-volume-weighted estimate across sampled journals was 66.7% (95% CI, 64.0%-69.2%), and trends were insensitive to specification of false-positive rate in baseline data. The proportion of abstracts showing signs of AI-generated text was lower in journals with higher impact factors and higher in fully open-access journals. Conclusions: Estimated prevalence of AI-generated text increased substantially across all sampled medical journals, with marked between-journal differences associated with journal impact factor and publication model. These findings support development of standardized, transparent AI reporting in medical publishing.

items.title: Epidemiology and Antimicrobial Resistance of Klebsiella pneumoniae at a Tertiary Oncology Centre in Astana, Kazakhstan, 2022-2026: A Prospective Longitudinal Surveillance Study
items.abstract_or_text: Background. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a World Health Organization (WHO) critical priority pathogen, and carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae (CRKP) causes 50,000-100,000 attributable deaths annually worldwide. Systematic antimicrobial resistance (AMR) data from Central Asia are virtually absent from the global literature. Methods. Longitudinal surveillance study of routine microbiological data from the National Research Oncology Centre (NROC), Astana, Kazakhstan (January 2022-March 2026). Four data sources were integrated: monthly microbial landscape reports (October 2022-September 2024; n=596 K. pneumoniae isolates), a full-year patient-level clinical register (2025; n=91 isolates), monthly landscape reports for first quarter 2026 (Q1 2026 n=50 isolates), and biannual antibiograms (2022, 2026). Isolates were classified as CRKP (4MRGN), 3MRGN, ESBL-producing, or susceptible. Results. A total of 737 K. pneumoniae isolates were identified across the full study period. CRKP (4MRGN) was the dominant phenotype throughout, peaking at 76.4% in January-September 2024 and remaining at 62.0% in Q1 2026. The aggregate MDR rate (CRKP + 3MRGN + ESBL) was 76-87% across all periods, consistently 2-3 times above the global pooled mean of 28.7%. The highest resistance burden was observed in the bone marrow transplantation department (86-98% MDR) and intensive care units (67-100% MDR). Between 2022 and 2026, a profound shift in reserve antibiotic susceptibility was documented: amikacin resistance rose from 8.5% (2022) to 38.1% (Q1 2026, whole institution) and 60% (Q1 2026, intensive care sector), nearly eliminating the sole previously active antibiotic class. In contrast, polymyxins (colistin R 0%, polymyxin B R 2%) and tigecycline (R 52%) emerged as the only agents with retained activity in 2026. Carbapenem resistance showed a modest partial improvement (meropenem R 72%-85%) but remained critically high. Simultaneously, Escherichia coli (ESBL+/MDR) emerged as the dominant pathogen in haematological and surgical departments by 2025-2026, reflecting a broader Enterobacterales resistance crisis beyond K. pneumoniae alone. Conclusions. This study provides the first systematic published AMR surveillance evidence from Kazakhstan over a four-year period. CRKP dominates the institutional microbiological landscape, and the progressive loss of aminoglycoside activity now leaves polymyxins and tigecycline as the last remaining active agents-a development with profound implications for patient safety. These findings represent a critical call to action for antimicrobial stewardship implementation, carbapenemase genotyping, and integration into national and global AMR surveillance systems in Central Asia. Keywords: Klebsiella pneumoniae; CRKP; carbapenem resistance; amikacin resistance; polymyxin; antimicrobial resistance; Kazakhstan; Central Asia; AMR surveillance; oncology

items.title: A latent space thermodynamic model of cell differentiation
items.abstract_or_text: Inferring the governing dynamics of differentiation that capture cell state evolution remains a central challenge in single-cell biology. We present Single-Cell Latent Space Dynamics (scLSD), a thermodynamics-inspired framework that models cell differentiation as evolution on a learned Waddington landscape in latent space. scLSD jointly infers a low-dimensional cell state, a differentiable potential function governing developmental flow, and a local entropy term that associates with cellular plasticity. Using a neural ordinary differential equation, scLSD reconstructs continuous differentiation trajectories from time-ordered single-cell data. Across diverse developmental systems, scLSD accurately recovers lineage hierarchies, predicts fate commitment for unseen cell types, and outperforms existing trajectory inference approaches in directional and cell fate prediction accuracy. In silico gene perturbations reveal how individual regulators reshape the landscape, and the proposed entropy measure is informative of plasticity in development and cancer.

items.title: Sequence-only antigen context improves modeling of antibody hypervariable regions
items.abstract_or_text: The complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) of antibodies govern antigen specificity; consequently, CDR design should be performed conditional on the target antigen. Most published approaches depend on the availability of the antigen's three-dimensional (3D) structure, which is often difficult to obtain experimentally. In contrast, sequence-only models circumvent this requirement but are typically trained on antibodies without incorporating antigen context; exposure to antigen sequences alone does not necessarily entail learning the underlying interaction determinants. Here, we introduce LangAAI, a masked language model that conditions exclusively on antibody and antigen primary sequences and therefore does not require 3D structures, docking poses, or epitope annotations. To assess whether the model exhibits genuine antigen conditioning, we replace the cognate antigen with a non-binding decoy. Whereas antigen-agnostic models are largely insensitive to this substitution, LangAAI shows a marked reduction in sequence recovery that is specifically concentrated in the hypervariable CDR3 loop. Across benchmarks, LangAAI improves amino-acid recovery relative to existing antibody language models, matches the performance of structure-based methods when evaluated under their respective protocols, and ranks experimentally measured variants by affinity comparably to inverse-folding models that use backbone coordinates. Collectively, these results support LangAAI as a structure-independent approach for antigen-aware antibody optimization, enabling prioritization of candidate variants for targets lacking solved antigen-antibody complexes.

items.title: Network Localization of Anxiety as an Early Manifestation of Alzheimer's Disease-related Neurodegeneration
items.abstract_or_text: Objective Anxiety is a prominent neuropsychiatric symptom in preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the neural circuitry linking anxiety and AD remains uncharacterized. We assessed whether anxiety in preclinical AD is independently associated with AD-related neurodegeneration and localizes to a common anxiety network. Methods In cognitively unimpaired (CU) older adults with 3T MRI and amyloid-beta PET (N=1,775), we examined whether an established AD-related atrophy network is associated with anxiety (STAI-6). Then, using Atrophy Network Mapping (ANM), which maps individual cortical atrophy patterns onto a normative functional connectome (N=1000), we derived an anxiety network. We tested its 1) spatial convergence with the AD network and with a causal anxiety network derived from lesion and neuromodulation data, 2) specificity relative to depression, 3) generalizability in samples from independent cohorts with AD and Parkinson's disease (total n=878), and 4) association with longitudinal outcomes. Results In CU older adults, greater AD-network atrophy was associated with higher anxiety, independent of depression, cognition, cortical atrophy, and amyloid burden. Anxiety localized to a network closely resembling the AD network (r=0.74, p=0.04) and the causal anxiety network (r=0.72, p=0.02). This convergence extended across the AD continuum and to the Parkinson's disease cohort and was specific to anxiety relative to depression. Greater anxiety-network atrophy was associated with cognitive decline over 4.6 years. Conclusion Anxiety localizes to a brain circuit resembling the AD-related atrophy network, is consistent across the AD continuum and may extend beyond AD. These findings support anxiety as an independent marker of early AD-related neurodegeneration.

items.title: Examining hearing-aid benefit during story listening in older adults using large language models
items.abstract_or_text: Hearing-aid benefit is typically assessed with isolated sentences, whereas everyday listening involves continuous speech. Yet, scoring comprehension of such speech can be labor-intensive. Here, we examined whether large language models (LLMs) can assess speech intelligibility and story comprehension in older hearing-aid users, and identify who benefits from hearing aids. Thirty-nine older adults (median age: 75 years) listened to sentences and short stories in multi-talker babble, under aided and unaided conditions. LLM-based intelligibility scores were nearly identical to established, rule-based scores. LLM-based intelligibility, gist, and detail recall scores were sensitive to masking and hearing-aid use. On average, hearing aids improved sentence intelligibility and story recall. Benefits increased with poorer hearing and, independently, with greater audibility gains from hearing aids. However, about half of the participants showed little benefit, primarily those with milder (though still clinically significant) hearing loss or smaller improvements in audibility. The results demonstrate that benefits of hearing aids for sentence intelligibility extended to comprehension of short stories and that LLMs enable automated assessment of both.

items.title: The neural basis of flavour-nutrient learning
items.abstract_or_text: Animals learn about the external world, in part, via interoceptive signals1,2. For example, the nutrient content of food is first estimated in the mouth, in the form of flavour, and then measured again via slower signals from the gut. How these signals from the mouth and gut are integrated to drive learning is unknown. Here we identify a dopamine pathway that enables learning about the nutrient content of food. We show that dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA-DA) are necessary for associating nutrients with flavours, and that post-ingestive nutrients trigger DA release selectively in a small region of the anterior basolateral amygdala (BLA) but not canonical DA targets in striatum. This nutrient-triggered DA release occurs preferentially in the left BLA in mice, and this same structure is preferentially activated by post-ingestive nutrients in humans. We identify the gut sensors that are responsible for nutrient-triggered DA release; show that they activate BLA-projecting DA neurons defined by expression of cholecystokinin (CCK); and demonstrate that stimulation of DA axon terminals in the anterior BLA drives flavour-nutrient learning but not other aspects of feeding behavior. Two-photon imaging of neurons in the left anterior BLA reveals that they integrate gustatory and post-ingestive cues, and silencing these neurons prevents flavour-nutrient learning. These findings establish a neural basis for how animals learn about the nutrient content of their food.

items.title: Engineered proteins to restore and enhance neurotransmitter release
items.abstract_or_text: Synapse dysfunction is a hallmark feature of many neurological diseases. Synaptic transmission is initiated in nerve terminals, where active zone protein complexes control vesicle fusion for neurotransmitter release. Here, we engineer proteins that mediate active zone functions and demonstrate their use for reconstituting and strengthening neurotransmission. A protein composed of CaV{beta}4 and the RIM1 zinc finger, {beta}4-Zn, restored neurotransmitter release after active zone disruption through recruitment of Munc13. We develop {beta}4-MC, derived from the Munc13-1 MUN and C2C domains, which bypasses Munc13 recruitment and directly mediates vesicle docking, priming and fusion after active zone disruption. In {beta}4-MC, MUN domain functions are dispensable for docking, but active MUN and C2C domains are both necessary for neurotransmitter release. In wild-type mouse and human neurons, {beta}4-MC but not {beta}4-Zn strengthens neurotransmitter release. Furthermore, {beta}4-Zn and {beta}4-MC restore and enhance dopamine release in the mouse striatum, respectively. Hence, {beta}4 proteins are engineered secretory proteins with therapeutic potential as enhancers of synaptic function.

items.title: Neurofibromin Regulates Sleep Consolidation via Cholinergic Neurons in a Drosophila Model of Neurofibromatosis 1
items.abstract_or_text: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) patients frequently present with fragmented, poor-quality sleep, but the neural circuits and molecular mechanisms underlying this deficit remain undefined. Using Drosophila, we show that loss of the NF1 ortholog dNf1 recapitulates the human phenotype: null mutants exhibit markedly reduced total sleep with blunted nighttime consolidation, reflected in fewer and shorter sleep bouts and elevated inter-bout activity, a recessive phenotype reproduced by independent null alleles and by pan-neuronal RNAi knockdown. Despite the broad expression of dNf1 across the adult CNS, including the mushroom bodies, ellipsoid body, dorsal fan-shaped body, and GABAergic neurons, cell-type-restricted knockdown showed the protein is dispensable for sleep regulation in each of these populations. Instead, dNf1 loss specifically in cholinergic neurons, the most abundant neuronal class in the fly brain, was sufficient to reproduce the deficient, fragmented sleep of null mutants, and restoring wild-type dNf1 to cholinergic neurons of null animals was both necessary and sufficient to rescue sleep. Mechanistically, cholinergic expression of the GAP-related domain (GRD) alone, which normalizes elevated Ras/MAPK signaling, fully restored sleep in nulls, whereas a catalytically dead GRD variant did not, establishing Ras/MAPK dysregulation in cholinergic neurons as the proximate cause. Two disease-associated missense mutations, dNf1C1045Y and dNf1R1861C, produced distinct, dose-graded sleep phenotypes. dNf1C1045Y showed severe deficits resembling the null and was resistant to pan-neuronal, but responded to cholinergic neuron-restricted rescue, consistent with a dominant-negative effect on dNf1 dimerization. In contrast, dNf1R1861C presented a milder phenotype that was largely reversible by wild-type dNf1 but only partially by the GRD domain, implicating an additional, GRD-independent mechanism. Collectively, these findings define cholinergic neurons as the key circuit through which Neurofibromin regulates sleep consolidation via Ras/MAPK signaling and reveal mutation-specific mechanisms that mirror the phenotypic heterogeneity seen in NF1 patients, with implications for genotype-informed understanding of sleep disturbance in this disorder.

items.title: A physics-informed neural network framework for inferring infinitesimal phase response curves from finite-pulse circadian recordings
items.abstract_or_text: Biological clocks reset and entrain to external cues in a phase-dependent manner. The infinitesimal phase response curve (iPRC) provides the local dynamical rule underlying this process by quantifying how an input changes the instantaneous phase velocity of an oscillator. Inferring iPRCs would make it possible to predict how rhythms respond to new stimulus timings and durations, but existing approaches often require detailed mechanistic models, long perturbation recordings, or specialized population-level resetting experiments. Here we introduce Physics-informed neural network for iPRC inference (PINN-iPRC), a physics-informed neural network framework for inferring iPRCs from standard finite-pulse stimulus-response recordings. PINN-iPRC represents the unknown iPRC as a neural network and embeds the phase equation into the loss function, identifying the iPRC that leads to the observed transient phase trajectory under the known stimulus. In synthetic oscillators, PINN-iPRC accurately recovered iPRCs from finite-pulse recordings, including complex ones that are difficult to capture with simpler parametric reconstructions. Applied to existing experimental Arabidopsis circadian recordings, PINN-iPRC recovered iPRCs comparable to those obtained from specialized population-level resetting experiments, while requiring only conventional stimulus-response trajectories. The inferred iPRCs were further used to predict finite-duration PRCs and circadian peak phases across photoperiods. In particular, the predicted near-invariance of the prr7 peak phase across 8-16 h of darkness was consistent with independently published prr7-11 root recordings. These results support PINN-iPRC as a practical physics-informed approach for extracting interpretable phase-sensitivity functions from routine biological oscillator recordings, with potential applications in experimental design, entrainment prediction, and chronotherapeutic or pharmacological schedule optimization.

items.title: Machine Learning-Derived Subtypes of Autism Reveal Distinct Genetic Contributions from Common and Rare Variants
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in core symptom severity and co-occurring conditions, complicating efforts to understand its genetic basis. Most genetic studies rely on binary case-control ASD definitions, which may obscure clinically meaningful variation and distinct genetic contributions across the autism spectrum. Methods: We constructed machine learning (ML)-based categorical ASD subtypes and corresponding continuous ASD subtype scores using 14 key clinical symptom measures with adjustment of sex and age among 6,355 autistic children in the Simons Foundation Powering Autism Research for Knowledge (SPARK) cohort by Discriminative Dimensionality Reduction via learning a Tree (DDRTree). We then replicated and validated these subtypes and scores among 2,717 autistic children in the Simons Simplex Collection (SSC) using a modified k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) approach. In SPARK and SSC, we further clinically validated the framework by examining associations of subtype classifications and scores with support needs, service utilization and medication use by regression models with adjustment for sex, age, genetic ancestry and socioeconomic factors. We further assessed SNP-based heritability, cell-type-specific heritability enrichment, polygenic scores (PGS) for psychiatric and cognitive traits, as well as rare copy-number variant (CNV) and de novo variant (DNV) burdens across the ML-derived ASD subtype scores adjusting for sex, age and genetic ancestry. Results: We identified three clinically distinct ASD subtypes in SPARK varying in the types of supports utilized: a high-support-needs (HSN) subtype characterized by broad developmental and functional impairments and very substantial support needs (OR = 1.63, P = 3.71 x 10-98); an emotional-behavioral-support-needs (EBSN) subtype marked by severe repetitive behaviors, elevated psychiatric comorbidity; and a low-support-needs (LSN) subtype with milder symptoms and relatively lower overall support needs. The three groups were associated with differential patterns in the specific types of treatments that were most common for them, from higher intensity to lower intensity. Projected ASD subtypes and scores in SSC recapitulated the phenotypic and medication-use patterns observed in SPARK. SNP-based heritability was highest for the EBSN score (h2g = 0.224, SE = 0.051) followed by the HSN (h2g = 0.167, SE = 0.049) and LSN score (h2g = 0.064, SE = 0.044), with suggestive cell-type-specific heritability enrichments in fetal endodermal cells and adult motor neurons for EBSN score and fetal excitatory neurons and astrocytes for HSN score (both P < 0.05). PGS of ADHD and major depressive disorder were consistently associated with higher EBSN scores in both SPARK and SSC. Higher DNV and rare CNV burden were associated with higher HSN score in SPARK, and higher rare CNV burden was associated with higher EBSN score in SSC (P < 0.05). Conclusions: Our ML-based transferable ASD subtype framework captured clinically and genetically meaningful dimensions of ASD heterogeneity, warranting further validation in larger cohorts. Keywords: Autism spectrum disorder, phenotypic heterogeneity, subtypes, machine learning, genetic burden

items.title: Relevance-Based Prediction: A Transparent, Patient-Specific Approach to Predicting Medical Outcomes
items.abstract_or_text: Accurate prediction of individual medical outcomes is essential for optimizing treatment allocation amid rising costs, coverage denials, and limited clinical resources. Traditional predictive models, including linear regression and neural networks, rely on average effects and cannot tailor predictions to the specific circumstances of individual cases. We present relevance-based prediction (RBP), a model-free and task-specific method that predicts outcomes as weighted averages of observed cases, with weights determined by a rigorously defined and theoretically justified measure of relevance. Unlike model-based methods that rely on fixed calibrated parameters, relevance-based prediction revisits the original data for each prediction and customizes both the cases and variables used. We illustrate RBP by applying it to predict opioid treatment outcomes and demonstrate that it provides case-specific insights unavailable from conventional models, including how each prior case informs a prediction, how each variable affects each predictions reliability and value, and how reliable each prediction is before it is made. These individualized insights may prevent misleading average-based decisions and reduce harmful or suboptimal treatment.

items.title: Hypervirulent Listeria isolated from a wild rabbit in Canada.
items.abstract_or_text: Listeria monocytogenes is the causative agent of listeriosis, a major foodborne disease with a 30% mortality rate in humans. Although L. monocytogenes can infect animals, whether wildlife can serve as a reservoir remains understudied, especially in Canada. Here, we characterized an L. monocytogenes strain (W0463-24) extracted from a wild cottontail rabbit ( Sylvilagus floridanus ) submitted to the Canadian Wildlife Health Cooperative at the University of Guelph. The rabbit had severe swelling of the head, multiple scabs around the muzzle and eyes, and was diagnosed with disseminated lymphoma, multifocal necrotizing hepatitis with gram-positive bacteria, and nematodosis. Liver and spleen were PCR-negative for Francisella tularensis , and liver was 4+ for L. monocytogenes on bacterial culture. Whole-genome analysis characterized isolate W0463-24 as sequence type 1 (ST1), clonal complex 1 (CC1), and lineage I. Multiple virulence and stress response genes were identified in silico, including the Listeria pathogenicity island 3 (LIPI-3). Invasion of human colon adenocarcinoma (Caco-2) cells in vitro was significantly greater with W0463-24 compared with wild-type strain 10403S. We found that this ST1, CC1, lineage I wildlife isolate has high pathogenic potential, emphasizing wildlife both as potential reservoirs and as populations vulnerable to L. monocytogenes infection.
